newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi aims to detail Italy Euro-tax within a week.
newsitem.headline: Prodi aims to detail Italy Euro-tax within a week.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Monday he aimed to spell out the details of a planned "Euro-tax" contained in his 1997 austerity budget within a week.
"I will announce the Europe contribution when we have worked it out," Prodi told an interviewer on state television RAI.
"I hope to do that within a few days -- about a week."

The centre-left government's budget, which is scheduled to face its final vote in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) this week, aims to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's deficit.
Prodi has announced plans to levy 12.5 trillion lire via a one-off tax to help ensure Italy is in shape to join Europe's planned Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) at its start in 1999.

Newspaper articles have speculated that middle-class Italians could be hard hit by the tax. Up to 500,000 people, far more than expected, joined a demonstration in Rome at the weekend led by opposition centre-right leader Silvio Berlusconi against Prodi's planned tax hikes.
Berlusconi's centre-right Freedom Alliance and the separatist Northern League party vowed earlier to boycott Thursday's scheduled final vote on the budget in the Chamber.

They oppose the tax hikes and particularly object to special powers contained in the budget bill that would allow the government to set policy on sensitive matters, including tax, without the need to keep going back to parliament for approval.

Asked what the cost of the Euro-tax would be for the average Italian, Prodi said: "The biggest price would be the one we will pay if we don't get in (to EMU). It would be a kind of tragedy with the risk of financial tragedy and an undervalued lira..."
"The tax for Europe will not cost much," he added.
Prodi used the interview to offer publicly to tighten his own belt financially by vowing not to use a special fund of one billion lire a year set aside for the prime minister.
"That sum has not been touched, even though I would be entitled to," he said, though he admitted he did not know whether all of his ministers were following suit. ($1=1515 Lire)
